newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch Holec plans stock exchange comeback in 1988.
newsitem.headline: Dutch Holec plans stock exchange comeback in 1988.

text.p: Dutch engineering group Holec Holland, formerly an Amsterdam Stock Exchange listed company, said on Wednesday it planned to return to the bourse.
"The plan is to seek a listing for Holec during the second half of 1998," chairman Guido Declercq told Reuters, adding the firm was currently preparing the ground for such a move.
"We are planning a float in Amsterdam in 1998, provided that the bourse climate is not bearish," Declercq said, adding he did not rule out a listing in New York and London as well.
Declercq, who is also a member of Holec's supervisory board, said he planned to stay on as chairman when the firm was admitted to listing.
He will be replaced on the supervisory board, as Dutch stock exchange listings requirements do not permit simultaneous executive and supervisory posts.
"I shape and reshape companies," Declercq said. "I was taken on board in April 1995, and I will stay on at least until the bourse launch has successfully been completed."
Holec, established in 1962 through the merger of several small engineering companies, was listed on the Amsterdam stock Exchange throughout the Eighties.
In 1990 it was taken over by Begemann Groep NV, but the relationship was short-lived.

In 1994 Holec's overhead power cables unit Holec Hoogspanning was sold to Austrian Elin. A year later UBS Equity, a unit of Union Bank of Switzerland, bought Holec International, transforming it into Holec Holland.
UBS currently owns 55.6 percent of Holec Holland. Venture capital firm CINven owns 40.9 percent, while Holec's management has 1.4 percent and the employees of Holec hold 2.1 percent.
"All the shares, or nearly all, will be floated," Declercq said.
Group turnover is expected to rise to 340 million guilders ($198.9 million) in the current year from 320 million guilders in 1995 and 300 million in 1994.
Operating profits are set to surpass 30 million guilders in 1996, Declercq said.
Holec Holland posted an operating profit of some 25 million guilders in 1995, following the deconsolidation and closure of several loss-making units.
"The French unit of Holec was making a loss of one million guilders per month and unfortunately there are 12 months in a year," Declercq said.
The French unit is currently under court protection from creditors, while loss-making Polish unit Bat Muskau and power supply unit HPP were both closed down.
The slimmed-down Holec Holland employs 1600 people.
Declercq said the firm was not entirely ready for a stock exchange listing in the near future.
"We have to show a good track record first," he said.
Declercq said margins should be at least 11 percent and the return on assets should be 16 percent.
He said he saw steady growth possibilities in Eastern Europe and the Far East.

About 60 percent of Holec's turnover is derived in the Dutch home market. Foreign markets include Denmark and Sweden. The firm recently said it planned to start a joint venture in China for the production of medium voltage switch-gear systems.
Declercq said Holec was seeking a partner for its unit Holec Algemene Toelevering BV, which distributes machinery parts to the other two Holec divisions, Holec low voltage and Holec medium voltage.
"We want to maintain a 25 percent-plus-one (share) holding in Holec Algemene Toelevering (HAT), Declercq said.
The 25 percent-plus-one stake would safeguard Holec's right of veto in major decisions affecting HAT, he explained.
Holec group companies currently use 80 percent of HAT's turnover of components versus 94 percent before.
"We want to increase sales to outside firms," Declercq said, adding Holec was targeting an increase in third party sales to 35 percent.
Declercq declined to name any candidates for a joint venture with HAT.
